title: Enumerations and Type Aliases
relevance: Enums and typedef aliases replace magic integers with named, intent-revealing types that interviewers check when assessing readable C++ fundamentals.

phases.goal: Establish what enumerations and typedef aliases are and the readability problem they solve.

must_hit.point: An enumeration defines a new type whose values are a named, fixed set of constants.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says an enum introduces a type limited to a fixed set of named member constants.

must_hit.point: Raw integer encodings of fixed choice sets (menus, days, suits, ratings) are easy to mistype and hard to read; enums map readable names to small integer codes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts magic numbers with named members for small fixed choice sets.

must_hit.point: typedef introduces a new name for an existing type; the aliased name is not a new type, only another spelling of the original that documents intent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states typedef is an alias spelling, not a distinct type, used to document meaning.

probes: What problem do enumerations solve that raw integer codes do not?
What does typedef actually create — a new type, or something else?

hints.1: Think about menus, days of the week, or card suits written as bare numbers.
hints.2: An enum names a fixed set of constants as a type; typedef only renames an existing type.
hints.3: Enum = new type with a fixed named constant set; typedef = another spelling of an existing type that documents intent.

phases.goal: Show how enum members are numbered by default and with explicit values, and how typedef aliases are declared.

must_hit.point: An enum lists members in braces; by default they are numbered automatically from zero in order (e.g. mon = 0 through sun = 6).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes enum day { mon, tue, ... } and assigns 0, 1, 2, ... in declaration order.

must_hit.point: Any member may be given an explicit value; later members without an explicit value continue counting up from the most recent one (e.g. mon = 1, tue = 2, wed = 5, thur = 6, fri = 7, sat = 9, sun = 10).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains continuation from the last explicit value with the day example values.

must_hit.point: typedef int marks and typedef int rollno make marks and rollno simply int under another name at the point of declaration.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows typedef int marks; typedef int rollno; and treats both as int.

probes: If mon = 1 and wed = 5 with no values on tue, thur, and fri, what values do those members get?
How do you declare a typedef alias for int used as marks?

hints.1: Default numbering starts at the first member; explicit values change where counting resumes.
hints.2: After an explicit value, the next unnamed members are last+1, last+2, and so on.
hints.3: mon = 1 ⇒ tue = 2; wed = 5 ⇒ thur = 6, fri = 7; sat = 9 ⇒ sun = 10; typedef int marks; typedef int rollno;

phases.goal: Contrast named enums and typedef aliases with bare machine types for readability without changing computation.

must_hit.point: Both enumerations and typedef aliases improve readability without changing what the program computes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says they clarify intent but leave runtime behaviour the same as using the underlying integers/types.

must_hit.point: An enum variable can have only the listed set of values and expresses intent in comparisons (d == mon) instead of a magic number (d == 0).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate prefers d == mon over d == 0 and notes the value set is restricted to the enum members.

must_hit.point: marks and rollno aliases leave behaviour identical to using int throughout while making declarations self-describing about what the integers represent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says marks/rollno are still int but declarations state marks vs roll numbers.

probes: Why prefer an enum member name in a comparison over comparing against 0?
If marks and rollno are both typedefs for int, what changes about program behaviour versus using int directly?

hints.1: Focus on readability and intent, not on different machine instructions.
hints.2: Enum comparisons name the choice; typedef only documents what an int is for.
hints.3: d == mon beats d == 0 for intent and allowed values; marks/rollno behave exactly like int but read as marks or roll numbers.

phases.goal: Apply enum variables and typedef aliases in simple program declarations and control flow.

must_hit.point: A variable of enum type (e.g. day d or dep d) may be assigned listed members and used directly in expressions and comparisons such as if (d == mon).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate declares day d or dep d, assigns mon/fri/sun or ece, and compares with == mon.

must_hit.point: With typedef int marks and typedef int rollno, you can declare marks m1, m2, m3 and rollno r1, r2, r3 to show what those integers store.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate declares marks and rollno variables to label marks vs roll-number ints.

probes: Write a small main that declares a day, assigns fri, and checks whether it equals mon.
How would you declare three marks variables and three roll-number variables using typedef aliases?

hints.1: Declare a variable whose type is the enum or typedef name, then assign and compare.
hints.2: day d; d = fri; if (d == mon) { ... } and marks m1, m2, m3; rollno r1, r2, r3.
hints.3: Full pattern: enum day { mon, ... }; day d = fri; if (d == mon) {}; typedef int marks; typedef int rollno; marks m1, m2, m3; rollno r1, r2, r3.

tradeoffs.topic: enum named members vs magic integer codes
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Enums keep a fixed named set and let comparisons read as intent (d == mon) instead of opaque codes (d == 0), without changing what the program computes.

tradeoffs.topic: typedef alias names vs bare int
tradeoffs.strong_answer: typedef marks/rollno are still int — not new types — but declarations document whether values are marks or roll numbers while behaviour stays identical to int.

gotchas.trap: Assuming every enum member must be given an explicit integer value.
gotchas.correction: Only some members need explicit values; any that follow without one continue counting up from the most recent explicit value.

gotchas.trap: Treating a typedef name as a distinct new type that the type system separates from the original.
gotchas.correction: typedef only introduces another spelling of an existing type; marks and rollno are simply int.

gotchas.trap: Writing comparisons against raw codes like d == 0 when the enum members are available.
gotchas.correction: Use the member name (d == mon) so the code expresses intent and stays tied to the allowed value set.
